readerTitle: Why Quaker's $1.7 billion Snapple plan fell apart
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Quaker Oats의 Snapple 인수, 1994~1997) + 인수 성과 연구의 일반적 결론 + 가상 적용 (스낵 제조사, 업무관리 소프트웨어)
insight: 시너지는 '합치면 좋아진다'는 형용사가 아니라, 누가 무엇을 바꾸는지 적을 수 있는 구체적 메커니즘일 때만 진짜다. 우리가 통제하는 비용 시너지는 믿을 만하고, 고객·유통사가 행동을 바꿔야 하는 매출 시너지는 검증 전까지 상상에 가깝다.
misconception: 두 회사의 강점을 합치면 시너지는 자연히 생긴다. 우리 유통망과 마케팅이면 인수한 브랜드도 저절로 커진다.

sources.text: Quaker Oats의 Snapple 인수(1994, 약 17억 달러)와 Triarc에 매각(1997, 약 3억 달러) 관련 당시 언론 보도 (The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal 등)
Christofferson, S., McNish, R., & Sias, D. (2004). Where mergers go wrong. McKinsey Quarterly.

factChecks.note: 인수가 약 17억 달러(1994년), 매각가 약 3억 달러(1997년, Triarc)는 널리 인용되는 수치입니다. 게시 전 당시 보도로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 'about'으로 적었습니다.
Quaker가 Gatorade의 대형 매장 유통 시스템으로 Snapple을 밀려 했고, Snapple은 독립 유통사를 통해 편의점·델리 등 소형 매장에서 냉장 단품으로 주로 팔렸다는 설명은 여러 사례 분석에 나옵니다. 세부 내용(유통사 반발 정도)은 출처로 확인하세요.
Snapple의 특유한 광고(이른바 'Snapple Lady')를 Quaker가 바꿨다는 내용은 보도된 내용이라 카드에 'reportedly'로 적었습니다. 확인 필요.
'매출 시너지가 비용 시너지보다 더 자주 빗나간다'는 결론은 McKinsey(2004) 등에서 나온 일반적 결론입니다. 구체 비율은 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다. 원문으로 표현이 맞는지 확인하세요.
가격 손실 계산: 17억 − 3억 = 약 14억 달러 차이. 카드에는 차이 수치를 따로 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Bought for $1.7 billion. Sold for $300 million.
body: In 1994, Quaker Oats, the maker of Gatorade, bought the iced-tea brand Snapple for about $1.7 billion.
About three years later, it sold Snapple for roughly $300 million. The plan looked brilliant on paper. The trouble was where the plan lived: only on paper.

image.label: A tall stack of money shrinking to a small pile beside a juice bottle
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 높은 지폐 더미(1994), 오른쪽에 작게 줄어든 지폐 더미(1997), 가운데 라벨 없는 아이스티 병. 실제 브랜드 로고와 병 디자인은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which promised gain will actually show up?
body: You run a snack maker whose trucks deliver to big supermarkets. You're buying a craft drink brand that sells mostly in corner shops and cafés.
Your team lists three synergies. Which one are you most confident in?

options.text: Our supermarket trucks will double their drink's sales
options.feedback: It sounds like the biggest win, but it depends on supermarkets stocking it and their shoppers wanting it. Neither is in your control.

options.text: Buying sugar, bottles and cartons together gets us better prices
options.feedback: Smaller on paper, but you control it. You can call suppliers before the deal closes and get real quotes.

options.text: Our marketing team will make their brand much bigger
options.feedback: Possible, but your team knows supermarket shoppers. The brand's fans may like it precisely because it isn't a big-company product.

cards.title: The trucks went to the wrong stores.
body: Quaker's plan was to push Snapple through the system that made Gatorade huge: big deliveries to supermarkets.

But Snapple lived somewhere else. Independent distributors delivered cold single bottles to delis, gas stations and corner shops. Those distributors had their own interests and didn't want to give up the business.
Quaker also reportedly replaced Snapple's quirky advertising. Meanwhile, rival iced teas crowded the shelves. The growth the deal was priced on never arrived.

cards.title: Real vs imagined synergies
body: A **synergy** is value two businesses create together that neither could create alone.

A **real synergy** has a specific mechanism: you can say what changes, who does it and how you'd measure it. An **imagined synergy** is a hope that customers, partners or staff will act differently from how they act today.
Quaker's distribution synergy needed delis, distributors and shoppers to change. That made it imagined, however large it looked.

image.label: Two columns: gears that connect versus a thought bubble
image.brief: 두 칸 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 'Real' 칸에는 서로 맞물린 톱니바퀴와 체크리스트(What changes / Who / How measured). 오른쪽 'Imagined' 칸에는 생각 풍선 안의 화살표와 물음표.

cards.title: Costs you control. Revenue you hope for.
body: Most synergies fall into two kinds.
list: **Cost synergies:** one warehouse instead of two, joint purchasing, shared trucks. Mostly inside your control.
**Revenue synergies:** cross-selling, new channels, a bigger brand. These depend on other people's choices.
cards.callout: Studies of past deals, including McKinsey's 2004 review, found revenue synergies are missed more often than cost synergies.
cards.softwareNote: Merging two companies' server bills and support tools is a cost synergy you can plan. "Our users will also buy their product" is a revenue synergy until you see users actually buy it.

cards.title: Real doesn't mean free, and imagined doesn't mean impossible.
body: Cost synergies carry one-time costs: moving systems, severance, lost staff. Cutting too much can also remove the thing that made the business worth buying.
And some revenue synergies do happen. The safer move is to test them before paying for them: sell to a small group of customers first, or pay the seller more only if the growth arrives.

image.label: A scale weighing savings against integration costs
image.brief: 저울 일러스트. 한쪽에 'Savings' 동전 더미, 다른 쪽에 'Integration costs' 상자와 떠나는 직원 실루엣. 저울이 거의 수평.

cards.title: Now it's a software deal.
body: Your project-management software company wants to buy a small time-tracking app. The banker's model says 30% of your customers will add it, which justifies a high price. The seller wants an answer this month.

options.text: Pay the high price. The fit is obvious and the model is careful
options.feedback: A careful spreadsheet is still a guess about customer behavior. If only 5% add it, you've overpaid for growth you never got.

options.text: Price it on cost savings, and pay extra only if cross-sales hit a target
options.feedback: You pay for what you control and share the risk on what you don't. You may lose the deal if the seller won't accept it.

options.text: Walk away. Revenue synergies never work
options.feedback: You avoid overpaying, but you may miss a good deal. Testing a revenue synergy beats either believing or rejecting it.

cards.title: A synergy is only real if you can say who changes what.
body: Pay for the gains you control. Test, or share the risk on, the ones that need customers and partners to behave differently.
**Try it today:** take one partnership or deal you're considering. For each promised benefit, write who has to change what. Circle any line where that person isn't you.
